lesson.text: Quick memory: how did people probably move Stonehenge's giant stones? (On wooden sledges pulled with ropes.) Now a new material arrives: metal.
People found that some rocks, heated in a very hot fire, gave out shiny metal. Getting metal out of rock like this is called smelting. The first metal used much was copper.
Copper is soft. Then metalworkers found that melting copper with a little tin made a much harder metal: bronze. It is about 9 parts copper to 1 part tin.
Melted bronze was poured into moulds of stone or clay. When it cooled, out came an axe, a knife, a pin or a bowl. A broken tool could be melted and made again!
Metalworking reached Britain about 4,500 years ago. Copper was mined deep under the Great Orme in Wales, and tin came from Cornwall.
Copper and tin were rarely found in the same place, so people traded: metal, amber, gold and pots travelled far. The Dover Boat, about 3,500 years old, may have crossed the sea to France.
The Bronze Age happened at different times in different places. In Egypt, Mesopotamia and China, bronze was used by great kingdoms that also built cities and wrote.
Try it in the world: build a Bronze Age workshop with a furnace, and a trading post by the river where Tilly can swap metal for grain.

exercises.prompt: Bronze is made by mixing copper with which metal?
exercises.hint: Remember the table: two soft metals make one hard one.
exercises.explain: Bronze is copper mixed with a little tin: about 9 parts copper to 1 part tin.

exercises.hint: Why would metalworkers bother to mix in tin?
exercises.explain: True: copper is soft, but copper and tin together make hard bronze.

exercises.hint: It starts with rock and a very hot fire.
choices: heating rock to get metal out of it
exercises.explain: Smelting is heating rock (ore) in a very hot fire so the metal comes out.

exercises.prompt: Bronze tools were made by pouring melted metal into moulds.
exercises.hint: Think of a jelly mould: the shape of the mould becomes the shape of the jelly.
exercises.explain: True: melted bronze was poured into stone or clay moulds and left to cool.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for making a bronze axe in order.
exercises.hint: You need the rocks first, and the shape comes last.
items: pour it into an axe mould
dig up copper and tin rocks
smelt the rocks to get the metals
melt and mix copper and tin
exercises.explain: Dig up the rocks, smelt them, mix the melted copper and tin, then pour the bronze into a mould.

exercises.prompt: Why did trade grow in the Bronze Age?
exercises.hint: To make bronze you need two metals. Were they found together?
choices: copper and tin came from different places
exercises.explain: Copper and tin were rarely found in the same place, so people traded to get both.

exercises.prompt: Where in Britain was tin mined?
exercises.hint: It is in the far south-west of England.
exercises.explain: Tin came from Cornwall; copper came from places like the Great Orme in Wales.

exercises.prompt: A broken bronze tool could be melted down and made into a new one.
exercises.hint: What happens to bronze in a very hot fire?
exercises.explain: True: bronze can be melted and poured into a mould again, so nothing was wasted.

exercises.prompt: Why was bronze better than stone for an axe?
exercises.hint: What happens to a stone axe if you drop it on a rock?
choices: it could be sharpened again and did not shatter
it was lighter than a feather
exercises.explain: Bronze does not shatter like stone, and a blunt edge can be sharpened again.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
items: iron tools are made in Britain
bronze tools are made in Britain
exercises.explain: Flint tools (Stone Age), farming villages (New Stone Age), then bronze, then iron.

exercises.prompt: The Bronze Age began at the same time all over the world.
exercises.explain: False: bronze was made earlier in some places than in others.

exercises.prompt: A Bronze Age grave in England held gold from far away. What does it tell us?
exercises.hint: How could gold from far away get there?
exercises.explain: Things from far away show that people traded or travelled over long distances.

exercises.prompt: Bronze is about 9 parts copper to 1 part tin. A smith has 18 kg of copper. How much tin is needed?
exercises.hint: For every 9 kg of copper you need 1 kg of tin. How many 9s are in 18?
exercises.explain: 18 is two 9s, so the smith needs 2 × 1 = 2 kg of tin.

exercises.prompt: Match each metal to what it is like.
matches: soft, mined at the Great Orme
exercises.hint: Two of them are soft, and one is made by mixing the other two.
exercises.explain: Copper (soft, from the Great Orme) and tin (soft, from Cornwall) mix to make hard bronze.

exercises.prompt: Sort the facts: copper, tin or bronze?
exercises.hint: Copper came from Wales and tin from Cornwall; mixed, they make bronze.
exercises.explain: Copper: mined at the Great Orme, 9 parts in every 10 of bronze. Tin: mined in Cornwall, 1 part in 10. Bronze: harder than copper, and poured into moulds for axes.

exercises.prompt: Bronze is 9 parts copper to 1 part tin. A smith has 27 kg of copper. How many kg of bronze can she make?
exercises.hint: Find the tin first: 1 part for every 9 parts of copper. Then add the two.
exercises.explain: 27 kg is three 9s, so she needs 3 kg of tin. 27 + 3 = 30 kg of bronze.
